title: Big hospital, small hospital
concept: Small samples vary more: a small hospital has more days with over 60% boys than a big one, even though each birth is 50/50.
kept: Hospital pair, and the question of which has more days with over 60% boys
Student's first guess ('about the same') offered as a choice
Simulate a year of births in both hospitals and count the days
Hospital theme with baby blue and pink
filled_in: Hospital sizes: 15 and 45 births a day (the classic version of this problem), chosen because the design gave none
Opening, middle and end of the flow (left blank): guess, run a year, click days to inspect, 'Why' step, then sliders and reruns, then takeaway
One square per day, clickable to show that day's boys and girls
Sliders for each hospital's size and a table of past years as the explore step
'Over 60%' is strict: exactly 60% (9 of 15, 27 of 45) does not count, shown on screen

changed.what: Student's expectation 'probably the same' is treated as the common wrong answer, not the result
changed.why: The math says the small hospital has more such days: need 10+ boys of 15 (about 15% of days) vs 28+ of 45 (about 7% of days). Page shows the computed counts and compares the guess honestly.

math_check: A day is over 60% when boys*5 > 3*n (exact integers). Minimum boys = floor(3n/5)+1: 10 of 15 and 28 of 45. Expected rates from the binomial: P(X>=10 | n=15) = 0.151, P(X>=28 | n=45) = 0.068, so about 55 vs 25 days a year. Page counts are computed from the simulated days with MK.rng; the checker ran the page with no errors and sample runs (e.g. 45 vs 23 days, 42 vs 21) match these rates. Point-per-baby values (100/n) and percentage ranges are computed from the data.
